title: Divergent ALMT functions underpin aluminum tolerance and growth in woody plants
content: Aluminum (Al) is the third most abundant element on the Earth's crust, primarily existing as insoluble and nontoxic form (eg, aluminosilicates) when soil pH is above 5.5. However, in acidic soil (pH <5), Al is solubilized into toxic trivalent form (Al3+), which is ready taken up by plant roots. This uptake induces oxidative stress and cellular damage and impairs root elongation, photosynthesis, and nutrient water uptake, ultimately reducing crop productivity (Kochian et al. 2015; Ofoe et al. 2023). To cope with Al3+ toxicity, many Al-sensitive plants species rely on several well-characterized strategies. For instance, Arabidopsis thaliana and wheat (Triticum aestivum) exude organic acids into root rhizosphere. These organic acids, such as malate and citrate, chelate Al3+ and render it less harmful. Their secretion is respectively mediated by aluminum-activated malate transporters (ALMTs) and multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) proteins (Kochian et al. 2015). Alternatively, other species, like rice (Oryza sativa), sequestrate Al3+ internally for detoxification: Al3+ is taken up into root cell by nramp aluminum transporter 1 (OsNrat1) across plasma membrane and then stored in vacuoles via OsALS1, an ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters/aluminum sensitive 1 (Kochian et al. 2015). Additional mechanisms, such as callose deposition at plasmodesmata, help restrict Al3+ movement between cells, partially mitigating Al toxicity, as reviewed in Ofoe et al. (2023) and Li et al. (2023).
